newsitem.title: DUBAI: YEAREND - Gulf-watchers see another year of tension.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Gulf-watchers see another year of tension.

text.p: The United States is still struggling to tame its arch-enemies in the Gulf and its most important regional ally is beset by internal challenges it seems reluctant to confront.

Analysts and diplomats expect more surprises from Iran and Iraq despite Washington's dual containment policy, and further anti-American violence in Saudi Arabia, the linchpin of U.S. foreign policy in a volatile region.
All three Gulf states hold keys to regional stability and the uninterrupted flow of oil to the industrialised world at stable prices.
All three suffered problems that spilled over into the region in 1996 and next year is likely to be equally turbulent, the analysts and diplomats say.

Iran defied U.S. sanctions in an attempt to break free of Washington's economic straitjacket, Iraq's President Saddam Hussein again demonstrated his ability to influence events beyond his own borders, and Saudi Arabia faced life with an aged and infirm king and more deadly violence against Americans.
PREDICTIONS

In 1997 Gulf analysts expect Iran to continue to seek deals with Central Asian republics, Russia and Turkey in defiance of U.S. trade and investment sanctions opposed by many countries, in particular Iran's key business partners in Europe and Japan.
An election in the Islamic republic will produce a new president but is unlikely to result in any radical change in the government or its policies, analysts say.
In Iraq, they expect Saddam will again try to expose rifts in the U.S.-led coalition which expelled his occupation army from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia is likely to face more violence including bombings by dissident Islamists opposed to Western influence in one of the world's most closed societies.

Although Crown Prince Abdullah's succession to King Fahd seems clear, what happens after that is murky. Many Saudis are coming to terms with what a Gulf-based diplomat called a crisis of expectations among a people used to lavish handouts now facing prices forced higher by reduced state subsidies.

Next July's presidential election in Iran will see the departure of Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, unable to run for a third term, as head of state but not necessarily from the scene. There is speculation that some prominent but as yet undetermined role as elder statesman will be found for him.
Frontrunner in the campaign to succeeed him as president is parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, who takes a tougher line towards the United States.
"There's no expectation that there will be a radical change of regime, only in degrees of pragmatism," said Middle East expert Rosemary Hollis.
INVESTOR WORRIES
But potential investors were still frightened off by U.S. pressure on Iran over alleged sponsorship of terrorism and Washington's accusation that it wants to become a nuclear power.

"People are not going to make big commitments in Iran for the time being until they see how this secondary boycott arrangement works. So everything's on hold with Iran," said Hollis, head of the Middle East programme at the London-based Royal Institute for International Affairs.
The European Union's critical dialogue with Iran was still alive, and both Germany and France were suggesting the Americans join them and get on with a managed policy towards Iran.
"The United States has offered dialogue at any time with an official of the Islamic republic," said a U.S. official who asked not to be named.

"This is not new U.S. policy. But the Iranians have never been able to pick up the glove. They're afraid of what's going to happen in Iran if they do. It could be the unravelling of the great revolutionary edifice if they talk to "the Great Satan'."
WEST NEEDS NEW POLICY ON IRAQ
Hollis said Baghdad was expected to come up with another surprise before long. "It would not be seen as in the nature of Saddam Hussein to just steer quietly into the distance."
But after action against Kurds in northern Iraq in August drew a U.S. armed response that was condemned elsewhere in the Gulf no-one dares speculate where that surprise will occur.

"Saddam exposed differences in the Western coalition and he'll try that again. He's shrewd. He'll go on poking the coalition to see if it will fall apart," said a European diplomat with long experience of the Gulf.

The West had to find a new policy on Iraq, the diplomat said. "We can't go on as we are. We are in for a period of re-evaluation on Iraq. The West must rethink policy on Iraq and keep up efforts to maintain dialogue with Iran. Dual containment is not a viable long-term policy."

Although the benefits of a United Nations deal allowing Iraq limited oil sales to pay for food and medicine are imminent, Iraqis face probably their toughest winter since U.N. sanctions were imposed after Saddam's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Iraq's return to oil markets is a challenge to Saudi Arabia and other key producers who could see lower returns after a year of unforeseen high prices and unbudgeted windfall profits.
CONCERNS OVER SAUDI ARABIA
Potentially more serious is the threat posed by dissident Islamists opposed to the Saudi royal family.
"The real threat in the Gulf now is not really Iraq or Iran but internal opposition (in Saudi Arabia)," said a Western arms executive who knows the region well.

Saudi Arabia -- austere, conservative and closed against the world with strict codes of behaviour enforced by Islamic morality police -- is key to whether the Gulf Arabs' system of rule will survive, said an ambassador with long experience of the kingdom and its neighbours.
"Will the Saudi regime survive 25 years from now? It's certainly 50-50. But beyond that it's questionable," he said.

"It's an incredibly repressive society -- trying to keep the world out, training thousands of graduates in Koranic studies which are useless for anything in the modern world. There's a limit to how many preachers and interpreters of the Koran you can have.
"There's a big question mark in the long term over the Saudi regime -- an army takeover or Iranian-style fanatics would send the most awful shock-waves around this part of the world."
Jane's Intelligence Review discounts the prospect of an Iranian-style revolution but says the kingdom risks internal political decay and socio-economic atrophy if it cannot reform.
Barring any progress with economic and social reforms, internal dissent was only likely to intensify, it said in a special report on Saudi Arabia.

And since the royal family was dependent on the United States and its European allies to guarantee the kingdom's security, the Western presence provided a target for militant Islamic groups opposed to the House of Saud.

"Since the current Saudi leadership is unlikely -- and strategically unable -- to ask the USA and its allies to leave, bombings such as those in Riyadh in November 1995 and Dhahran in June 1996 are likely to continue," it said.
